content.text: Hummingbirds are birds native to the Americas and comprise the biological family Trochilidae. With approximately 375 species and 113 genera,

they occur from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, but most species are found in Central and South America. Hummingbirds are known by that name because of the humming sound created by their beating wings, which flap at high frequencies audible to other birds and humans.

blocks.alt: Adult male bee hummingbird (Mellisuga helenae), the world’s smallest bird, photographed in Cuba.

content.text: Hummingbirds have varied specialized characteristics to enable rapid, maneuverable flight: exceptional metabolic capacity, adaptations to high altitude, sensitive visual and communication abilities, and long-distance migration in some species. Among all birds, male hummingbirds have the widest diversity of plumage color, particularly in blues, greens, and purples.

Across the estimated 375 species, hummingbird weights range from as small as 2.0 grams (0.071 oz) to as large as 20 grams (0.71 oz). They have characteristic long, narrow beaks (bills) which may be straight (of varying lengths) or highly curved. The bee hummingbird — only 6 centimetres (2.4 in) long and weighing about 2 grams — is the world’s smallest bird and smallest warm-blooded vertebrate.

blocks.alt: Close-up of a ruby-throated hummingbird’s foot showing three forward-pointing toes and one backward-pointing hallux.

caption.text: Close-up of toe arrangement in a ruby-throated hummingbird foot.

content.text: Hummingbirds do not walk on the ground or hop like most birds, but rather shuffle laterally and use their feet to grip while perching, preening feathers, or nest-building.
